important consideration in managing, marketing and sustaining cultural attractions and des-

The purpose of this project was to formulate a comprehensive methodology, to then
apply it to Italian cultural sites, and provide technical support for cultural heritage develop-
ment and tourism management policies. This innovative approach uses a combination of
qualitative analysis and quantitative indicators to tackle the main elements of tourist
ﬂows at the site, how visitation affects conservation, and how properties themselves
shape and in ﬂuence the visitor experience. This assesses the current negative or positive
element of the management system and provides site managers with guidelines for improv-
ing the tourism product while minimizing visitor impacts.
In this real-world research exercise, several case studies were chosen from Italian
museums and archaeological sites, two of which are described in this paper: the MAXXI
(National Museum of the arts of the XXI Century, in Rome) and the National Gallery of
Marche (Palazzo Ducale in Urbino). The project spanned two years (2011 and 2012) and
included the following:
. analyzing the state-of-the-art knowledge and practice of TCC and related methods
found in the literature;
. deﬁning indicators for providing a quantitative description of tourism’ s impacts;
. developing a speci ﬁc methodology to be applied to sites speci ﬁcally of cultural
interest;
. applying the methodology to real case studies and analyzing the results;
. drafting guidelines for managing tourist ﬂows; and
. disseminating the results.
Calculating TCC for cultural heritage sites
To assess cultural sites’ carrying capacity, the research team chose a method that could meet
the quantitative and qualitative needs of the project and provide useful guidance for the
implementation of future management plans. Two methods to evaluate TCC for heritage
places were implemented: a quantitative assessment of the impacts and a qualitative analy-
sis of the assets and visitor experiences. A further comparative review of the two and feasi-
bility veri ﬁcation brought about a mixed method that integrates quantitative aspects with
qualitative indicators. This synthetic model is innovative, as it is designed speci ﬁcally
for understanding cultural heritage. It is easy to apply and aims to provide useful guidelines
for proper site management.
The following section presents the two models separately and then applies them to
two case studies. Only the mixed methods approach was tested and applied, considering
that its ease of implementation would have contributed positively to an application at a
wider scale.
The quantitative method
The quantitative method is based on the application of Cifuentes ’ (1992) TCC method for
natural areas. It starts by calculating the physical carrying capacity, the value of which is
then corrected by applying a series of corrective coef ﬁcients derived from assessing the
social, infrastructural, environmental and psychological carrying capacity. The results of

RESEARCH NOTE
An application of tourism carrying capacity assessment at two Italian
cultural heritage sites
Elisabetta Cimnaghi a and Paola Mussini a,b*
aDIST – Dipartimento Interateneo di Scienze, Progetto e Politiche del Territorio (Interfaculty
Department in Territorial Science, Planning and Policies) Politecnico di Torino, c/o SiTI, via Pier
Carlo Boggio 61, Turin/Torino 10138, Italy; bCHIEF – Cultural Heritage International Emergency
Force, via Foscolo 20, Torino 10126, Italy
(Received 11 December 2013; accepted 7 November 2014 )
If not properly managed or organized, tourist ﬂows can constitute a risk for conserving
cultural heritage sites. It may therefore be important to estimate the maximum capacity a
visitor site can receive without compromising its heritage integrity or visitors ’
experiences. This research note formulates a comprehensive methodology to assess
the carrying capacity of cultural heritage sites as a way of providing technical support
for cultural development and tourism management policies. This approach proposes a
combination of qualitative and quantitative indicators to assess tourist ﬂows at a site,
how tourists affect conservation and how the property itself shapes and conditions the
visitor experience. This how-to study underscores the management system and
suggests guidelines to improve the tourism product without generating negative
impacts on the built heritage. Two museum case studies are highlighted – the
National Museum of the arts of the XXI Century, in Rome and the National Gallery
of Marche (Palazzo Ducale, in Urbino).
Keywords: tourism carrying capacity; cultural heritage; evaluation; National Gallery of
Marche; MAXXI; Italy
Introduction
This research note presents the results of a project developed by SiTi (Higher Institute for
Regional Systems for Innovation), a research institute based in Turin, in cooperation with
the Italian Ministry for Cultural Heritage, Activities and Tourism (MiBACT). It aims to
identify and analyze the impacts of tourism on cultural heritage sites, from both the conser-
vation and socio-economic points of view.
Presently, as far as the author is aware, no methodological approach has ever been
designed for calculating and, most importantly, properly managing tourist ﬂows at cultural
heritage sites. To this end, the most appropriate methodological framework is tourism car-
rying capacity (TCC), a theme which has been discussed at national and international
levels, but never leading to universal de ﬁnitions or measures. TCC is a quantitative
method used to identify the optimum number of tourists a particular destination is able
to sustain (Coccossis & Mexa, 2004; UNEP , 2003). The impacts of tourism at cultural

this evaluation are then compared to the actual managerial capacity of the site to assess
management carrying capacity, which ought to suggest solutions to identi ﬁed problems.
In particular, each component of the TCC is analyzed against a set of indicators; the cor-
rective coef ﬁcients are chosen by confronting the reference targets with the sites ’ actual
state of conservation.
The proposed indicators present four levels in relation to the reference targets:
. Level 1 – comparing indications provided by law (if present) or physical factors,
objectively measurable;
. Level 2 – comparing best practices as outlined in the literature;
. Level 3 – deﬁning site-speci ﬁc reference targets obtained after an advisory meeting
with the management body;
. Level 4 – qualitative indications, to be de ﬁned in consultation with the management
body.
Every element of the TCC is evaluated through a series of indicators, which are assessed
against reference targets and the actual state of conservation data. This produces the correc-
tive coefﬁcient. The integration of all corrective coef ﬁcients obtained for every TCC com-
ponent leads to the de ﬁnition of the weighted corrective coef ﬁcient that will be used to
decrease and update the physical TCC value (Table 1 ).
The qualitative method
To evaluate the site qualitatively, a form was designed to collect data and make
decisions about physical, environmental, social, psychological, infrastructural and man-
agement TCC. This kind of analysis aims to enrich a pure calculation merely based on
space used and size factors, with details on the very nature of the site considered and the
touristic experience offered, in terms of environmental comfort, services, support tools
and so on.
A second step of analysis follows wherein the evaluations are then confronted using a
matrix, returning a detailed framework of all the strengths and weaknesses of the system
and possible future scenarios. In particular, the matrix is differentiated depending on the
type of site considered (e.g. museum, archaeological site) and includes a series of indicators
for each component of the TCC. The ﬁnal evaluations are given for each TCC and weighted
after the preliminary information is collected in situ .
The mixed method
The two methods were integrated to comprise both qualitative and quantitative elements. It
was decided that each approach ’s most interesting elements would be considered to create a
ﬁnal analysis structure that would be used to assess of TCC in real-world cases, linking
quantitative indicators and qualitative assessment.
As a preliminary analysis, the so-called carrying capacity preliminary form was ﬁlled
out. This is a cognitive tool, able to underline the strengths and weaknesses of the
system and its peculiarities and main characteristics. The results help provide guidelines
for the future management of cultural heritage sites.
The main objectives of the method are to create a repeatable procedure and investigating
system, to direct future management decisions and strategies, and to provide a simpler
upgradable method which can use desk research and onsite analysis.

specializing in art and architecture, a bookshop, a cafeteria, a bar/restaurant, galleries for
temporary exhibitions, performances and educational activities. The large public square
in front of the museum is expected to host art works and live events. It was designed as
a multidisciplinary space and committed to experimentation and innovation in the arts
and architecture.
For the TCC evaluation, desk research and onsite analysis were done to assess the
impacts of tourism and gage the potential for management. Results suggest that given
the number of tourists observed and the calculated TCC, the museum is under-utilized
10 times less that it could be used. As well, the museum has clear potential to host tempor-
ary exhibitions, especially given its large exhibition halls and meeting spaces. The assess-
ment also suggests that to increase visitor traf ﬁc, MAXXI should ﬁnd new marketing
strategies, such as agreements with hotels and networking with other cultural attractions.
Finally, road signage is poor in terms of quality and location. More high-quality signs
need to be erected in the vicinity of the museum and at strategic places in the city of
Rome to help orient visitors toward the site.
Conclusions
This research note presented two cultural heritage sites, both museums but very different
from an architectural, locational and visitor numbers ’ points of view. The ﬁrst one is a
sixteenth-century historical building, designed to be a noble residence and thus restricted
by its age, fragility of material and spatial layout. The main issue related to its ability to
host visitors is to strike the proper balance between conservation needs and accessibility
for all.
Though dif ﬁcult to reach compared to other destinations in Italy, Urbino and Palazzo
Ducale are visited every year by many tourists, thanks in part to annual exhibitions, num-
bering more than residents. Carrying capacity evaluations in this case hinge largely on
material conservation, managing overcrowding, structural overloading, overcoming archi-
tectural barriers and modifying existing systems (e.g. light and heat) to be able to meet the
comfort and satisfaction needs of visitors.
On the other hand, MAXXI is a modern building, constructed to host contemporary
art exhibits, planned and detailed with pathways and visual design with visitors in mind.
The TCC analysis primarily alludes to low visitor numbers. This is a result of both infra-
structural aspects – the site is located outside the usual tourist area in Rome and is rela-
tively dif ﬁcult to reach by public transport – and lack of a proper marketing strategy.
The museum is somewhat unknown by tourists and residents, and no signs indicate
its location nearby.
Both applications illustrate the usefulness of the suggested method to highlight the chief
management weaknesses of these cultural heritage locations, having a data collection struc-
ture that is easy to update and interpret and providing interesting and case-speci ﬁc results.
However, some critical points must also be noted. First, some types of information, such as
the number of visitors with disabilities or direct interaction with site managers (this activity
was supposed to be performed during the third year of project implementation) were not
available. Second, it is dif ﬁcult to pinpoint a comprehensive method to gather users ’
opinions and to de ﬁne psychological TCC. Owing to the limited resources and time avail-
able in this project, questionnaires were unfeasible. Systematic observations would likely
be more cost-effective and time-efﬁ cient, together with the use of online questionnaires
and a content analysis of guestbook comments.

. Management TCC is a comprehensive theme, responding to all issues tackled by the
other TCC types ’ indicators. It provides useful strategies in response to a site ’s pre-
viously highlighted weak points and suggests how to improve the management of
tourism.
The application of the methodology consists of two main phases. First, preliminary
information about each site, the visit area, its legal statues and the number of visitors per
year (carrying capacity preliminary form) is collection (Table 2 ). Second, the value of
the indicators of the carrying capacity indicators table, which is de ﬁned as aspects that
describe the carrying capacity, is calculated (Table 3 ). These two forms are completed
via desk research and onsite technical surveys. The accuracy of this analysis depends
largely on the amount of data available. This framework can be, in any case, implemented
in the future by site managers.
Application to the case studies
The National Gallery of Marche, Urbino
The ﬁrst application of the method was carried out at the Galleria Nazionale delle Marche ,
located in the historic Palazzo Ducale in Urbino, Italy. It hosts a collection of important
artistic masterpieces gathered from churches and convents around the region during the
nineteenth century (Carrier, 2003) and exhibited in an area of 27 rooms, including the base-
ment, an archaeological site and a pottery museum. It is a monument of exceptional cultural,
historical and architectural value, a celebrated palace, part of a UNESCO World Heritage
Site (Historic Centre of Urbino), and one of the most beautiful Renaissance residences in
Italy.
Following the desk work, an onsite survey was administered in March 2012 to assess
the effectiveness of tourist ﬂows, impacts and potentials, linked primarily to the high cul-
tural value embodied by the palace and the outstanding artistic quality of the works of art
conserved there. It is also the main attraction of the city of Urbino, and it is therefore reason-
able to conjecture that almost every tourist visiting Urbino also has an interest in visiting
Palazzo Ducale.
The TCC evaluation highlighted some important weak points. First, the ﬂow of tourists
is lower than maximum capacity. It may therefore be necessary to plan strategies to attract a
higher number of visitors, such as through partnerships with hotels and other cultural sites.
Second, the museum ’s signposting system is adequate, but there are no dedicated means of
transporting people from other parts of town to the Palazzo, so access is not easy. Policies to
improve this aspect should be considered. Third, the comfort level indoors is low – too cold
in winter and too hot in summer. Fourth, some parts of the museum cannot be accessed by
visitors with disabilities. For instance, the staircases to the second and underground ﬂoors
have no ramps, and there is no elevator to the second ﬂoor. Finally, there is currently no
system in place to collect tourists ’ opinions or observations.
MAXXI (Museum of the Arts of the XXI Century), Rome
The MAXXI is a national museum in Rome, Italy, dedicated to contemporary creativity
(Jasper, 2014). It is managed by a foundation established by the Italian Ministry of Cultural
Heritage and Activities and consists of two museums: “MAXXI art ” and “MAXXI archi-
tecture”. In addition, the MAXXI also features an auditorium, a library and media library

TCC is broken down into its most characteristic aspects that need to be calculated and
evaluated in order to come to a ﬁnal result. The following de ﬁnitions were comprised based
on a review of the TCC literature:
. Theoretical TCC is a simple geometric consideration regarding the maximum number
of tourists that can stay at the same time in a certain location, given the site ’s area and
supposing that each person will occupy 1 m 2 of space.
. Physical/functional TCC is the theoretical TCC with corrective coef ﬁcients (qualitat-
ive or quantitative) related to the physical or functional aspects of the site, such as
accessibility inhibitors, safety requirements (e.g. maximum visitors allowed at one
time) or architectural barriers. The physical/functional TCC value is lower than theor-
etical TCC by de ﬁnition.
. Social TCC describes residents’ perceptions of tourism. This evaluation includes impor-
tant elements, such as tourism seasonality, tourists’ behavior and numbers of visitors.
. Psychological TCC is linked to the perceptions of tourists about the sites they visit,
how they judge the level of services, perceive hospitality policies and assess proper
signposting.
. Infrastructural/spatial TCC is a wider spectrum evaluation, which includes the
environment around the site, the adequacy of infrastructure and transportation pol-
icies, numbers of parking spaces and factors speci ﬁc to the area.
